title: A US diesel export ban would trigger global stock drawdowns, cut US refinery utilisation and risk driving gasoline prices higher, Wood Mackenzie finds
gist: Wood Mackenzie models a US diesel export ban (floated after US retail diesel hit a record $6.51/gal) as self-defeating: ~700 kb/d of diesel/gasoil would fill PADD 3 storage in about a month, forcing 2+ million bpd of crude run cuts that push costs onto gasoline. Abroad, the ban would accelerate product stock draws, lift NW Europe diesel cracks ~27%, and leave China as the only holder of meaningful spare refining capacity, which it may choose not to deploy.

themes.theme: Diesel market backdrop and supply shocks

insights.claim: US retail diesel prices hit an all-time high of $6.51 per gallon on 21 September 2026 and kept rising, prompting some lawmakers to call for pausing diesel exports to prioritise domestic supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Record pump prices create real political risk of export restrictions; watch legislative moves as a catalyst for refiners and product spreads.
insights.quote: US retail diesel prices hit an all-time high of $6.51 per gallon on 21 September (and have continued to rise)
insights.locator: US retail diesel prices hit an all-time high

insights.claim: US diesel exports have risen 340 kb/d over the past six months versus the 2025 average, absorbing three successive supply losses: Middle East barrels lost after the Strait of Hormuz closure, Russian diesel exports lost from mid-July 2026, and a lower crude supply outlook.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: The US has become the global diesel swing supplier; any curb on US exports removes the main buffer against stacked geopolitical supply shocks.
insights.locator: US diesel exports have risen 340 kb/d

insights.claim: Europe's share of US diesel/gasoil exports has risen to almost 50% in September 2026, up from a 30% average through 2025, which makes Europe the market most exposed to a US export ban.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: European middle-distillate balances now depend heavily on US flows; a ban would transmit directly into European diesel prices.

themes.theme: US storage saturation and refinery run cuts

insights.claim: Under a US diesel export ban, about 700 kb/d of diesel and gasoil oversupply would be redirected into storage, filling PADD 3 (US Gulf Coast) inventories to maximum capacity in just over a month.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Storage fills fast, so the physical squeeze on Gulf Coast refiners would arrive within weeks of a ban, not months.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie finds that if a ban were enacted

insights.claim: After PADD 3 fills, diesel inventories in the rest of the US, including the structurally short PADD 1 East Coast region, would reach capacity in roughly five or more additional weeks under an export ban.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Domestic price relief from a ban would be short-lived before storage limits force supply-side cuts nationwide.
insights.locator: Inventories in the rest of the United States

insights.claim: Keeping US inventories below capacity under a diesel export ban would require crude run cuts of over 2 million bpd, which exceeds PADD 3's current crude imports of under 2 million bpd and so could force higher US crude exports and diversion of some crude imports.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A ban would cut US refinery utilisation sharply and push more US crude into export markets, which is bearish for domestic crude differentials and refiner volumes.
insights.locator: To prevent inventories from exceeding capacity

themes.theme: Self-defeating policy: cost shifts to gasoline

insights.claim: A US diesel export ban would likely raise costs for American consumers overall, because crude run cuts needed to manage diesel oversupply would reduce gasoline output and increase the volume and cost of gasoline imports.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Position for gasoline cracks and import demand to rise if an export ban gains traction; the political fix could backfire at the gasoline pump.
insights.quote: The irony of a US diesel export ban is that it would likely increase costs for American consumers

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie frames a diesel export ban as shifting the price burden from diesel to gasoline rather than removing it, so any diesel pump relief would come with higher gasoline pump prices.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Assess refined-product policy by its effect across the whole barrel, not one product; a diesel-gasoline spread trade depends on whether the ban happens.
insights.quote: a policy designed to bring relief at the diesel pump could end up driving prices higher at the gasoline pump

themes.theme: Global contagion: Europe and Latin America

insights.claim: A US diesel export ban would accelerate drawdowns of diesel and gasoil inventories outside the US, as displaced US supply fails to reach those markets and competition for non-US barrels intensifies.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Expect tighter global middle-distillate balances and backwardation if a ban goes ahead.
insights.quote: A ban on US diesel exports would increase competition for non-US barrels in an already tightly supplied market
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie's modelling shows global diesel

insights.claim: Under the US export ban scenario, NW Europe diesel cracks are forecast to rise 27%, because European refining is already at maximum utilisation with no spare capacity to absorb the loss of US barrels.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: European refiners running flat out would capture wider margins; European diesel consumers and importers face the price hit.

insights.claim: Latin America would struggle to replace lost US diesel, with Wood Mackenzie's modelling identifying China (+300 kb/d) and Russia (+190 kb/d) as potential sources, both significantly constrained and Russia already maintaining its own export restrictions.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Latin American importers face supply security risk and higher landed diesel costs if US exports are halted.

insights.claim: With Russia's diesel export ban and high European refinery utilisation, China is currently the only country with material spare refining capacity to replace lost US refinery throughput, but it may decide not to do so.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Chinese product export policy, such as export quotas, becomes a key swing factor for global diesel prices; watch Beijing's stance if the US restricts exports.
insights.quote: China is currently the only country with material spare refining capacity that could cover the loss of US refinery throughputs. However, China may well decide it is not in its interest to do this.
